Unprecedented gameplay, other fighting games cant even come closer including the game that white and red karate guys can throw blue balls.

Game can be played at any level. If you like you can just open arcade or treasure mode and just smash, or go to the world of competition of Tekken.

Sometimes fair sometimes unfair, sometimes outplayed, sometimes outplay your opponent, beat by chance , beaten by chance, adapt opponent gameplay play with your opponent.Shows you all aspects of competitive gameplay. Game has a depthness that you can improve yourself for a lifetime.Every move has an answer, every move sometimes even every step is risk and reward. Been playing Tekken around 25 years and everyday learning new stuff.

Only criticism could be about heat engagers always puts you to 50/50 situation but this applies to your opponent as well, increasing luck for both parties, sometimes it feels unfair but sometimes you can beat players better than you as well so fair enough.

As a gamer playing since commodore 64 for me this is one of the best game ever made in gaming history.

To preface: I am a complete newcomer to fighting games, all of my thoughts here are from the perspective of someone who has no frame of reference from previous Tekken games. The most I did before buying this game was watch some Youtube guides to understand the game's basic mechanics and if it looked like something I'd like to play.

Choosing between a positive or negative review was a difficult choice, I greatly enjoyed the core gameplay but there were many annoying things in the game that compounded into me ultimately going with a negative review. At one point I even uninstalled the game, only to reinstall it later just to get another fix (Which was excruciating since it's a 100+ GB game). Here are my thoughts on the game's various pieces in no particular order.

The Story - The story mode was the first thing I did in the game, and I was not very impressed. I watched all of the cutscenes summarizing previous games, but even with that the writing was simply abysmal. Extremely generic anime writing with very little depth to any of the characters. The whole thing took me maybe 4-5 hours to complete, so I'm sure a fighting game veteran would likely blitz through the whole thing. Annoyingly, the story mode did not offer much in the way of a tutorial, so most of my learning was pausing at the start of a fight and scrolling through the move lists. The character episodes were even less, you got a brief introductory cutscene, a few fights, than an end cutscene, without adding much more depth to the characters.

Arcade Quest - To be perfectly honest, arcade quest might as well have been the real story mode. It was better in basically every way. A more in-depth tutorial that focuses on whatever character you're playing, a sense of progression as you travel to different arcades fighting stronger and stronger bots (even if they're absolute garbage once you start learning your fundamentals). The writing is still generic as hell of course, but it was fun.

Tekken Ball - Tried it once, didn't care for it... that's all.

Fight Lounge - Seems like an interesting way to introduce a more social aspect to the game. You can chat with people, play against them over and over, and even practice with other players which is really cool. The main downside though is that playing against people is clunky, you have to go to a set of machines, go through a loading screen into a queue, to then "match" against the person. It's very awkward, slow, and unintuitive.

Customization - The customization is alright. I like the ability to freely change parts of an item/clothing to any color you want, and it's a feature I wish more character creators would adopt. The amount of items you can equip is a bit underwhelming, options for facial features like hairstyles and eye colors are especially limited, and the inability to add or tweak things on full body outfits feels rather restrictive. Still, it gives enough creative freedom to pull off some really good looking and/or goofy outfits, as well as cosplays.

Monetization - This is a $70 game. If it just had cosmetic microtransactions, I'd find it distasteful but ultimately not care too much since it would be just that, cosmetic. Unfortunately, this is not the case for Tekken 8. You have a battlepass, and paid characters and stages. Making people pay for decades-old characters in a $70 game is criminal, and I hate that ♥♥♥♥ like this is normalized in the gaming industry as a whole. Hell, the worst part for me is that you can't even choose the characters in practice mode if you don't own them, so you can't even lab them unless you have somebody willing to practice online with you.

Practice/Replays - The practice mode is phenomenal. The sheer amount of options and settings you can adjust allows you to practice any scenario, positioning, combo, punish, etc. Additionally, the ability to view replays, as well as take control while watching them is a fantastic. A very well thought-out mode.

Quickplay/Ranked - Okay, time for the real meat of the game. Starting out, I got my ass handed to me, as was expected. I slowly worked my way up to Garyu over the course of a few months as I learned a character or two, slowly working on my fundamentals and figuring out how to stop getting hit by stupid ♥♥♥♥. (Disclaimer: I still get hit by stupid ♥♥♥♥, and I cannot break throws, such is life.)

The learning process was extremely fun, getting a feel for the game's movement and applying more moves and combos into real matches was a blast. The ability to infinitely rematch in quickplay was a much needed addition, as it allowed me and a complete stranger to keep beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other while learning our characters' matchup, this was peak enjoyment of the game for me. Unfortunately, reaching the Garyu/Shinryu threshold is where issues with the game became more prevalent.

I understand that much of the game's population is within orange and red ranks, but the skill disparity just doesn't make sense. Sometimes I would get matched up against what felt like green ranks who didn't understand frames and just button mash as you obliterate them. Other times, I would get matched up against what felt like blue ranks who promptly beat my ass. They ducked every high and grab, blocked or parried every low, performed insane wall-carry combos, etc. I'm not sure if smurfing is that prevalent or red ranks are just THAT wide in the range of skill, but matches like these became so common that it just wasn't fun.

Additionally, reaching Garyu is where the game's aggressive nature became much more prevalent. I met more people that would just absolutely rush me down with characters like Nina, Heihachi, and Reina with constant plus on block strings and 50/50s. Now let me say, I understand that these are mostly knowledge checks. I understand that each of these characters have gaps where you can sidestep, jab, crouch, etc to get out of the rush. What I'm saying is that situations like these are where most of the fun vanished. I play games in my free time after work and weekends, I like Tekken 8, but I want to play other games too. For a single character to have the ability to completely shut you down unless you decide to go and lab them for extended periods of time feels ridiculous. It feels like red ranks are a wall that halts all of your momentum until you decide to start extensively labbing, it was a very sudden difficulty spike and smothered out a lot of the enjoyment I was having with the game.

Now, the above wouldn't bother me nearly as much if most of these issues didn't seep into Quickplay, but they do. Huge skill disparity, some characters forcing you to adapt or die, relatively common lagswitching and plugging. It all just feels like a coin toss as to whether or not I'm going to actually enjoy a match. (Also, WHY are people with 20%+ disconnection rates allowed to play the game without any penalties, and WHY don't you at least get a win on record whenever somebody DCs?)

Heat & Rage - I believe my problems with the aggressive gameplay are exacerbated by heat smashes and rage arts. The damage boost from rage as a comeback mechanic seems fine, what I HATE is rage arts. A fast, hyperarmor, high damage move that ignores all hits and throws and forces you to watch a cutscene is not fun. I've lost track of the amount of times where I get someone down to low health, and then the entire match turns into a spacing game of who's going to press the "win button" first. I don't like heat at all, the core gameplay already feels robust, but adding heat smashes and oppressive chip damage just takes away from the game.

As of this review I've uninstalled, I REALLY wanted to like this game, but the constant back-and-forth of enjoyment and annoyance has finally worn me down. Might play more, might not, but without a serious overhaul of the game's aggressive nature, I don't see myself playing much more of this game.

Tekken 8 is a flawed fighting game that leans into the modern formula with all of its weight. There is an abundance of offensive tools. Lots of plus frames, high damage combos, 50/50 mix-up situations and the core system mechanics heavily favour this play-style. Unfortunately not every player can fit into that play-style and it has become, in its most recent update, a slot machine but the result always yields 777 on the damage counter. With a few honest tweaks this game can achieve the greatness it strives to reach.

What Tekken 8 Does Well:
+Comprehensive and interactive tutorial in the form of Arcade Quest. You will create an avatar (which you will also use in the games online modes) to engage in a short story mode (approx. 3 hours in length) where you simulate going to local tournaments and as the story progresses you will learn the different layers to Tekken 8.

+Fully in-depth Training Mode. Complete with everything you'd expect from a fighting game with some modern era tweaks, such as Punishment Training. Frame data, combo trials, replay takeover, reset states, wake-ups, stage interactions. It's all there. You'd be hard pressed to find something this games training mode genuinely lacks. Tekken 8 gives you the tools and labbing has never been more fun for me personally.

+Ghost Mode. Another modern addition that enhances player experience. I personally used this in tandem with training mode almost exclusively for 9 months before regularly fighting my friends or playing opponents online. It takes the stress of learning out of the equation while not holding your hand (too tightly mind you) as a CPU would.

+Customisation is back and while its a step down from other games before it namely Tekken 7 and Soulcalibur 6, it does have pretty fun options. You can make almost anything and most customs encountered online are also in good taste. I have literally seen thousands of customs in this game. It definitely allows creative minds to flourish. But there is 100% room for improvement.

+Roster and DLC are quite good. I don't have too much to say about this one. I fortunately have all of my mains already available, though my main Lidia should have been on the launch roster. Coming from Soulcalibur I never cared about Bamco showing all of the DLC at once, because they have never done it like that. Modern sensibilities and economics dictate that more players want to know who exactly they are getting in each season so I understand players now wanting a shift from how Bamco does reveals. I think their current model of at least telling us if the character is returning, new, or guest is a fair middle ground. Bamco also said they would revisit this strategy pending more and more people asking for open reveals. Very fair.

+Music, the game launched with a very catchy OST of its own but also with a complete jukebox of music from the previous games. I especially like that if they use music from an older game like they did with the reveal of Anna Williams, I can just go and find that. I do mostly play with music off though, to help my concentration. Can't say too much here, but I think music is the least of anyones worries.

+Lots of player expression with titles, artwork, frames, banners, etc.
+Lots of single player content.

Things Tekken 8 can work on:
-Netcode can be shaky especially if one player is wired and one is playing on wifi. In fact, about 4 months after the games launch it has rejected all LAN cables I have tried to use. I'm not an elitist tho and will play with pretty much anyone. Netcode is usually part of the games skeleton and any changes to this framework is difficult to improve without disrupting the user experience. I get it. It's serviceable and way better than pre-covid titles. But it does leave more to be desired when you look at the rollback of other modern fighting games.

-The games core mechanic "HEAT" can feel overbearing in the sense that there is not much counterplay to it. You take increased damage off of Heat specific attacks, if you block an attack during Heat you will take chip damage, Heat dashes will leave you at disadvantage and will put you in a guess for game situation in many scenarios, Heat Smashes are "Level 1 type Supers" that will deal respectable damage if they connect, if they are blocked they will deal a decent amount of chip and will leave the defender at disadvantage and in yet another guess for game scenario. There just aren't enough defensive options. Game can feel like Street Fighter: Oops All Cammy's Edition sometimes. Heat in general I do not mind but it can use tweaks.

-Way too many moves give you plus frames. This makes it so that the game just plays like "Whoever Hits First WINS". There is not much room for neutral based gameplay because you will likely win neutral after your first interaction and won't relinquish it until you yourself make a mistake in your own gameplan. It can be very boring. And while I don't think combos are "too long" per se, I can understand the sentiment where the round ended quickly based off of two interactions "in neutral".

Overall I would rate Tekken 8 an 9/10. I thoroughly enjoy the game and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys fighting games. But I do want to make known that the game has its issues. Those issues aren't insurmountable and I do think the dev team will ultimately make the changes the game needs. I say this as a person who plays nearly everyday, with anyone, at any level and even in my local scene. Not as an emotional bot who is vocalising what a doomtuber or twitterhead told them to think. At the end of the day I do believe EVERYONE wants Tekken to succeed. I write this review mostly to catalog my own thoughts and encourage others to try the game and make their own judgements.

I remember when my friend first got me into Tekken 7. It was hard, very hard, and it was the first fighting game I had ever jumped into. We played it like a party game for months, practicing combos sometimes, and never really taking it seriously. I remember that day like it was yesterday as well, when I was at work and I was thinking about Lei Wulong, and I texted my friend that I wanted to commit to learning him. Fully learning him, down to the last string. And that was the day I created the Lei Bible for myself.

It took the better part of a year, but it was fun. I genuinely took months to learn everything about Lei, from his frame data to every move in every one of his stances. From his punishers to every one of his wall combos. I learned everything there was to learn about Lei, and I wrote them all by hand in a notebook of mine just so I could memorize and know Lei down to his core. With my friend's help and guidance, I learned and had Lei Wulong down to memory, and I dragged myself to Tekken God Prime with a character that the Tekken community thought was too complicated to play. It was gratifying, genuinely. I played honorably, ignoring dissent from some pros like TheMainManSwe who said that all you needed to do was spam Hellsweep and Razor Rush to climb rank. I wanted to earn a high rank off of my own skill and hard work, and before Tekken 8 came out, I beat that same friend who helped me become as great as I was, a Tekken God Omega Kazuya, in a first to 10 sparring tournament we held against each other. That was the first time I had ever beaten him in that game, and I was sure that as we both transitioned over to Tekken 8, the high I had felt that day would be felt many more times throughout the years. The high of honorably and respectfully winning a duel against an equally respectful and honorable opponent. Unfortunately, that spar we had would be the last time I ever felt high again.

Because Lei wasn't in the game at launch, I had to find a new main, and despite the fact that I had never liked Jin's playstyle when I had first started Tekken, his gameplay in Tekken 8 spoke to me now that I had a deep commitment to playing fair and honorable characters. Spamming, unfair advantages, and broken mechanics didn't make me feel like I earned a win against an opponent, and despite Jin being more flashy and bombastic in this game than he was in 7, I didn't feel like I had an unfair advantage above other opponents like I felt with other characters, so I chose him to be my main, and I learned him fast now that I knew what to learn. I learned everything there was to learn about him and committed myself to playing honest, and I was ready to get into ranked.

To cut to the chase, Tekken 8 just felt wrong. It wasn't the fact that new players were relentlessly spamming, something I devoted myself not to do. It wasn't the fact that any opponent had a built in unfair mechanic to just take your turn back after an opponent rightfully earned a punish, or the fact that anybody could throw out ultimates so easily that you'd get an entire round you earned the win on robbed from you because someone panicked and pressed one button. It wasn't even the fact that movement was heavily gutted, so I couldn't practice Korean Backdash to cause my enemy to wiff when they were being too aggressive. If it were just those things, I could have adjusted and adapted, changing my playstyle up so I could match their aggressiveness and keeping pace with my own. What made Tekken 8 feel so wrong was that all of this was heavily rewarded, while my honest playstyle was not. Spamming strings and moves you didn't understand the frame data for was now the new meta, and being honest was not a thing anymore. Anybody could just press any buttons instead of trying to be strategic and outsmart your opponent. Combos were a waste of time and barely did enough damage to matter. There wasn't respect in anybody's gameplay anymore. I never saw someone Korean Backdash and punish my wiff with a perfectly timed launcher, because that wasn't a thing anymore. I never saw someone notice that they used the same string twice in a row and backed off to clear their mind and not spam. Hell, I didn't even see anybody try to do flashy combos that required work. All that mattered was spamming and getting off a Heat Smash, and if the enemy gets you near death, spam Rage Art. Nobody needed to learn their character like it was back in Tekken 7. Nobody was trying to achieve victory, they just wanted to watch the opponent lose. 

And believe me, I defended the game when it first came out. However, as time wore on, I realized I never got that high that I got from Tekken 7. I never felt like I beat the opponent because I read their next move and beat them with my knowledge, I only ever beat them because they had no idea what I was doing. Tekken 8 lost so much of its identity, and I tried to voice my concern to the community, but I was met with dismissive comment from people brand new to the series who had jumped on the bandwagon and wanted to act like they knew what Tekken was like before. Criticism that could have helped the game got drowned out, and eventually I dropped Tekken 8, followed by my friend who couldn't stand what the game had become following close behind me. 

As a community, we feel dejected. Tekken is too easy now. They made every character beginner friendly but took out all of the hardest things in Tekken that you could learn. Player expression was gutted, as you probably have heard many people say, but its true. I've never seen someone in Tekken 8 do something that left me in awe and made me want to jump in and practice it, because its not difficult. Anybody who practices the game could do what any pro can currently do, and there's nothing skill-wise that can separate us. And unfortunately, our criticism and pleads didn't just get drowned out, but they got actively ignored by the developers. The devs only wanted to listen to the people who would sing Tekken 8's praise, and in response to everybody begging them to fix the game, they turned around and finished the job, thoroughly destroying the game with this second season. I'll admit, I haven't played the second season, so don't think I'm claiming something I'm not, but it doesn't require you to play it for you to know how bad their decisions were. They nerfed the already gutted movement system and doubled down on aggressive gameplay, to the point where you can't even sidestep mids. Oki is practically nonexistent. Defense is practically nonexistent. Its barely even a fighting game anymore. Its just a rushdown simulator, seeing who can press buttons faster than the other before their healthbars disappear. And the devs hear the outcries of their fanbase and would rather tell them to stop complaining, while thanking the few contrarians who defend the game who get proven to not even play it. 

Let's face it, if the devs don't want to hear from us, then they don't want us here. Fine by me. I treated Tekken like a party game in the beginning, but grew to respect it when I saw how much time and focus I could put into it to improve my gameplay. Now, all people do is treat Tekken like a party game, and they don't ever grow out of that mindset because they're rewarded for doing so. So maybe Tekken is a party game now. This isn't the game I dedicated over a year to improving myself on. That game was left behind, just like we have been now. Tekken is dead.

im recommending this game but know this:

its a guess fest. your opponent may very well be just mashing buttons and you still will be at disadvantage.

its a game that punishes defense. youre blocking, waiting for your turn and it never comes. you have to guess what attack will break your opponents chain based on their next move (that can be anything).

along with defending, rolling, side-stepping and any evasion methods from the previous games have been debuffed. 

if youre playing a female character, know that being faster dont mean ♥♥♥♥ against a male character. if they start first, they hit you, if you start first, they overpower your attack and hit you.

80% of the character roster dont stand a chance against 2 or 3 characters from the original roster and none of the new dlc characters.

and EVERY new character is a response to the roster. they will come with a chain that interrupts almost anything anyone has and/or break any established rule previously set and be overpowered against the everyone until the next new dlc.

yes, the music is better, the engine is beautiful and the player base may be larger (than tekken 7, for example - but not that much larger), but the amount of frustration you may get after an online match is considerate.

all that said, again: im still playing it. ive paid for it, after all. anyone saying "just get better" or "its just a noob complaint" is probably the ones exploring the unbalanced characters. what a great game if everyone is forced to play with the same character as everyone else just to have a chance.

We played it like a party game for months, practicing combos sometimes, and never really taking it seriously. I remember that day like it was yesterday as well, when I was at work and I was thinking about Lei Wulong, and I texted my friend that I wanted to commit to learning him. Fully learning him, down to the last string. And that was the day I created the Lei Bible for myself.

It took the better part of a year, but it was fun. I genuinely took months to learn everything about Lei, from his frame data to every move in every one of his stances. From his punishers to every one of his wall combos. I learned everything there was to learn about Lei, and I wrote them all by hand in a notebook of mine just so I could memorize and know Lei down to his core. With my friend's help and guidance, I learned and had Lei Wulong down to memory, and I dragged myself to Tekken God Prime with a character that the Tekken community thought was too complicated to play. It was gratifying, genuinely. I played honorably, ignoring dissent from some pros like TheMainManSwe who said that all you needed to do was spam Hellsweep and Razor Rush to climb rank. I wanted to earn a high rank off of my own skill and hard work, and before Tekken 8 came out, I beat that same friend who helped me become as great as I was, a Tekken God Omega Kazuya, in a first to 10 sparring tournament we held against each other. That was the first time I had ever beaten him in that game, and I was sure that as we both transitioned over to Tekken 8, the high I had felt that day would be felt many more times throughout the years. The high of honorably and respectfully winning a duel against an equally respectful and honorable opponent. Unfortunately, that spar we had would be the last time I ever felt high again.

Because Lei wasn't in the game at launch, I had to find a new main, and despite the fact that I had never liked Jin's playstyle when I had first started Tekken, his gameplay in Tekken 8 spoke to me now that I had a deep commitment to playing fair and honorable characters. Spamming, unfair advantages, and broken mechanics didn't make me feel like I earned a win against an opponent, and despite Jin being more flashy and bombastic in this game than he was in 7, I didn't feel like I had an unfair advantage above other opponents like I felt with other characters, so I chose him to be my main, and I learned him fast now that I knew what to learn. I learned everything there was to learn about him and committed myself to playing honest, and I was ready to get into ranked.

To cut to the chase, Tekken 8 just felt wrong. It wasn't the fact that new players were relentlessly spamming, something I devoted myself not to do. It wasn't the fact that any opponent had a built in unfair mechanic to just take your turn back after an opponent rightfully earned a punish, or the fact that anybody could throw out ultimates so easily that you'd get an entire round you earned the win on robbed from you because someone panicked and pressed one button. It wasn't even the fact that movement was heavily gutted, so I couldn't practice Korean Backdash to cause my enemy to wiff when they were being too aggressive. If it were just those things, I could have adjusted and adapted, changing my playstyle up so I could match their aggressiveness and keeping pace with my own. What made Tekken 8 feel so wrong was that all of this was heavily rewarded, while my honest playstyle was not. Spamming strings and moves you didn't understand the frame data for was now the new meta, and being honest was not a thing anymore. Anybody could just press any buttons instead of trying to be strategic and outsmart your opponent. Combos were a waste of time and barely did enough damage to matter. There wasn't respect in anybody's gameplay anymore. I never saw someone Korean Backdash and punish my wiff with a perfectly timed launcher, because that wasn't a thing anymore. I never saw someone notice that they used the same string twice in a row and backed off to clear their mind and not spam. Hell, I didn't even see anybody try to do flashy combos that required work. All that mattered was spamming and getting off a Heat Smash, and if the enemy gets you near death, spam Rage Art. Nobody needed to learn their character like it was back in Tekken 7. Nobody was trying to achieve victory, they just wanted to watch the opponent lose. 

And believe me, I defended the game when it first came out. However, as time wore on, I realized I never got that high that I got from Tekken 7. I never felt like I beat the opponent because I read their next move and beat them with my knowledge, I only ever beat them because they had no idea what I was doing. Tekken 8 lost so much of its identity, and I tried to voice my concern to the community, but I was met with dismissive comment from people brand new to the series who had jumped on the bandwagon and wanted to act like they knew what Tekken was like before. Criticism that could have helped the game got drowned out, and eventually I dropped Tekken 8, followed by my friend who couldn't stand what the game had become following close behind me. 

As a community, we feel dejected. Tekken is too easy now. They made every character beginner friendly but took out all of the hardest things in Tekken that you could learn. Player expression was gutted, as you probably have heard many people say, but its true. I've never seen someone in Tekken 8 do something that left me in awe and made me want to jump in and practice it, because its not difficult. Anybody who practices the game could do what any pro can currently do, and there's nothing skill-wise that can separate us. And unfortunately, our criticism and pleads didn't just get drowned out, but they got actively ignored by the developers. The devs only wanted to listen to the people who would sing Tekken 8's praise, and in response to everybody begging them to fix the game, they turned around and finished the job, thoroughly destroying the game with this second season. I'll admit, I haven't played the second season, so don't think I'm claiming something I'm not, but it doesn't require you to play it for you to know how bad their decisions were. They nerfed the already gutted movement system and doubled down on aggressive gameplay, to the point where you can't even sidestep mids. Oki is practically nonexistent. Defense is practically nonexistent. Its barely even a fighting game anymore. Its just a rushdown simulator, seeing who can press buttons faster than the other before their healthbars disappear. And the devs hear the outcries of their fanbase and would rather tell them to stop complaining, while thanking the few contrarians who defend the game who get proven to not even play it. 

Let's face it, if the devs don't want to hear from us, then they don't want us here. Fine by me. I treated Tekken like a party game in the beginning, but grew to respect it when I saw how much time and focus I could put into it to improve my gameplay. Now, all people do is treat Tekken like a party game, and they don't ever grow out of that mindset because they're rewarded for doing so. So maybe Tekken is a party game now. This isn't the game I dedicated over a year to improving myself on. That game was left behind, just like we have been now. Tekken is dead.

Tekken 8 is a flawed fighting game that leans into the modern formula with all of its weight. There is an abundance of offensive tools. To preface: I am a complete newcomer to fighting games, all of my thoughts here are from the perspective of someone who has no frame of reference from previous Tekken games. The most I did before buying this game was watch some Youtube guides to understand the game's basic mechanics and if it looked like something I'd like to play.

Choosing between a positive or negative review was a difficult choice, I greatly enjoyed the core gameplay but there were many annoying things in the game that compounded into me ultimately going with a negative review. At one point I even uninstalled the game, only to reinstall it later just to get another fix (Which was excruciating since it's a 100+ GB game). Here are my thoughts on the game's various pieces in no particular order.

The Story - The story mode was the first thing I did in the game, and I was not very impressed. I watched all of the cutscenes summarizing previous games, but even with that the writing was simply abysmal. Extremely generic anime writing with very little depth to any of the characters. The whole thing took me maybe 4-5 hours to complete, so I'm sure a fighting game veteran would likely blitz through the whole thing. Annoyingly, the story mode did not offer much in the way of a tutorial, so most of my learning was pausing at the start of a fight and scrolling through the move lists. The character episodes were even less, you got a brief introductory cutscene, a few fights, than an end cutscene, without adding much more depth to the characters.

Arcade Quest - To be perfectly honest, arcade quest might as well have been the real story mode. It was better in basically every way. A more in-depth tutorial that focuses on whatever character you're playing, a sense of progression as you travel to different arcades fighting stronger and stronger bots (even if they're absolute garbage once you start learning your fundamentals). The writing is still generic as hell of course, but it was fun.

Tekken Ball - Tried it once, didn't care for it... that's all.

Fight Lounge - Seems like an interesting way to introduce a more social aspect to the game. You can chat with people, play against them over and over, and even practice with other players which is really cool. The main downside though is that playing against people is clunky, you have to go to a set of machines, go through a loading screen into a queue, to then "match" against the person. It's very awkward, slow, and unintuitive.

Customization - The customization is alright. I like the ability to freely change parts of an item/clothing to any color you want, and it's a feature I wish more character creators would adopt. The amount of items you can equip is a bit underwhelming, options for facial features like hairstyles and eye colors are especially limited, and the inability to add or tweak things on full body outfits feels rather restrictive. Still, it gives enough creative freedom to pull off some really good looking and/or goofy outfits, as well as cosplays.

Monetization - This is a $70 game. If it just had cosmetic microtransactions, I'd find it distasteful but ultimately not care too much since it would be just that, cosmetic. Unfortunately, this is not the case for Tekken 8. You have a battlepass, and paid characters and stages. Making people pay for decades-old characters in a $70 game is criminal, and I hate that ♥♥♥♥ like this is normalized in the gaming industry as a whole. Hell, the worst part for me is that you can't even choose the characters in practice mode if you don't own them, so you can't even lab them unless you have somebody willing to practice online with you.

Practice/Replays - The practice mode is phenomenal. The sheer amount of options and settings you can adjust allows you to practice any scenario, positioning, combo, punish, etc. Additionally, the ability to view replays, as well as take control while watching them is a fantastic. A very well thought-out mode.

Quickplay/Ranked - Okay, time for the real meat of the game. Starting out, I got my ass handed to me, as was expected. I slowly worked my way up to Garyu over the course of a few months as I learned a character or two, slowly working on my fundamentals and figuring out how to stop getting hit by stupid ♥♥♥♥. (Disclaimer: I still get hit by stupid ♥♥♥♥, and I cannot break throws, such is life.)

The learning process was extremely fun, getting a feel for the game's movement and applying more moves and combos into real matches was a blast. The ability to infinitely rematch in quickplay was a much needed addition, as it allowed me and a complete stranger to keep beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other while learning our characters' matchup, this was peak enjoyment of the game for me. Unfortunately, reaching the Garyu/Shinryu threshold is where issues with the game became more prevalent.

I understand that much of the game's population is within orange and red ranks, but the skill disparity just doesn't make sense. Sometimes I would get matched up against what felt like green ranks who didn't understand frames and just button mash as you obliterate them. Other times, I would get matched up against what felt like blue ranks who promptly beat my ass. They ducked every high and grab, blocked or parried every low, performed insane wall-carry combos, etc. I'm not sure if smurfing is that prevalent or red ranks are just THAT wide in the range of skill, but matches like these became so common that it just wasn't fun.

Additionally, reaching Garyu is where the game's aggressive nature became much more prevalent. I met more people that would just absolutely rush me down with characters like Nina, Heihachi, and Reina with constant plus on block strings and 50/50s. Now let me say, I understand that these are mostly knowledge checks. I understand that each of these characters have gaps where you can sidestep, jab, crouch, etc to get out of the rush. What I'm saying is that situations like these are where most of the fun vanished. I play games in my free time after work and weekends, I like Tekken 8, but I want to play other games too. For a single character to have the ability to completely shut you down unless you decide to go and lab them for extended periods of time feels ridiculous. It feels like red ranks are a wall that halts all of your momentum until you decide to start extensively labbing, it was a very sudden difficulty spike and smothered out a lot of the enjoyment I was having with the game.

Now, the above wouldn't bother me nearly as much if most of these issues didn't seep into Quickplay, but they do. Huge skill disparity, some characters forcing you to adapt or die, relatively common lagswitching and plugging. It all just feels like a coin toss as to whether or not I'm going to actually enjoy a match. (Also, WHY are people with 20%+ disconnection rates allowed to play the game without any penalties, and WHY don't you at least get a win on record whenever somebody DCs?)

Heat & Rage - I believe my problems with the aggressive gameplay are exacerbated by heat smashes and rage arts. The damage boost from rage as a comeback mechanic seems fine, what I HATE is rage arts. Unfortunately not every player can fit into that play-style and it has become, in its most recent update, a slot machine but the result always yields 777 on the damage counter. With a few honest tweaks this game can achieve the greatness it strives to reach.

What Tekken 8 Does Well:
+Comprehensive and interactive tutorial in the form of Arcade Quest. You will create an avatar (which you will also use in the games online modes) to engage in a short story mode (approx. 3 hours in length) where you simulate going to local tournaments and as the story progresses you will learn the different layers to Tekken 8.

+Fully in-depth Training Mode. Complete with everything you'd expect from a fighting game with some modern era tweaks, such as Punishment Training. Frame data, combo trials, replay takeover, reset states, wake-ups, stage interactions. It's all there. You'd be hard pressed to find something this games training mode genuinely lacks. Tekken 8 gives you the tools and labbing has never been more fun for me personally.

I personally used this in tandem with training mode almost exclusively for 9 months before regularly fighting my friends or playing opponents online. We played it like a party game for months, practicing combos sometimes, and never really taking it seriously. I remember that day like it was yesterday as well, when I was at work and I was thinking about Lei Wulong, and I texted my friend that I wanted to commit to learning him. Fully learning him, down to the last string. And that was the day I created the Lei Bible for myself.

It took the better part of a year, but it was fun. I genuinely took months to learn everything about Lei, from his frame data to every move in every one of his stances. From his punishers to every one of his wall combos. I learned everything there was to learn about Lei, and I wrote them all by hand in a notebook of mine just so I could memorize and know Lei down to his core. With my friend's help and guidance, I learned and had Lei Wulong down to memory, and I dragged myself to Tekken God Prime with a character that the Tekken community thought was too complicated to play. It was gratifying, genuinely. I played honorably, ignoring dissent from some pros like TheMainManSwe who said that all you needed to do was spam Hellsweep and Razor Rush to climb rank. I wanted to earn a high rank off of my own skill and hard work, and before Tekken 8 came out, I beat that same friend who helped me become as great as I was, a Tekken God Omega Kazuya, in a first to 10 sparring tournament we held against each other. That was the first time I had ever beaten him in that game, and I was sure that as we both transitioned over to Tekken 8, the high I had felt that day would be felt many more times throughout the years. The high of honorably and respectfully winning a duel against an equally respectful and honorable opponent. Unfortunately, that spar we had would be the last time I ever felt high again.

Because Lei wasn't in the game at launch, I had to find a new main, and despite the fact that I had never liked Jin's playstyle when I had first started Tekken, his gameplay in Tekken 8 spoke to me now that I had a deep commitment to playing fair and honorable characters. Spamming, unfair advantages, and broken mechanics didn't make me feel like I earned a win against an opponent, and despite Jin being more flashy and bombastic in this game than he was in 7, I didn't feel like I had an unfair advantage above other opponents like I felt with other characters, so I chose him to be my main, and I learned him fast now that I knew what to learn. I learned everything there was to learn about him and committed myself to playing honest, and I was ready to get into ranked.

To cut to the chase, Tekken 8 just felt wrong. It wasn't the fact that new players were relentlessly spamming, something I devoted myself not to do. It wasn't the fact that any opponent had a built in unfair mechanic to just take your turn back after an opponent rightfully earned a punish, or the fact that anybody could throw out ultimates so easily that you'd get an entire round you earned the win on robbed from you because someone panicked and pressed one button. It wasn't even the fact that movement was heavily gutted, so I couldn't practice Korean Backdash to cause my enemy to wiff when they were being too aggressive. If it were just those things, I could have adjusted and adapted, changing my playstyle up so I could match their aggressiveness and keeping pace with my own. What made Tekken 8 feel so wrong was that all of this was heavily rewarded, while my honest playstyle was not. Spamming strings and moves you didn't understand the frame data for was now the new meta, and being honest was not a thing anymore. Anybody could just press any buttons instead of trying to be strategic and outsmart your opponent. Combos were a waste of time and barely did enough damage to matter. There wasn't respect in anybody's gameplay anymore. I never saw someone Korean Backdash and punish my wiff with a perfectly timed launcher, because that wasn't a thing anymore. I never saw someone notice that they used the same string twice in a row and backed off to clear their mind and not spam. Hell, I didn't even see anybody try to do flashy combos that required work. All that mattered was spamming and getting off a Heat Smash, and if the enemy gets you near death, spam Rage Art. Nobody needed to learn their character like it was back in Tekken 7. Nobody was trying to achieve victory, they just wanted to watch the opponent lose. 

And believe me, I defended the game when it first came out. However, as time wore on, I realized I never got that high that I got from Tekken 7. I never felt like I beat the opponent because I read their next move and beat them with my knowledge, I only ever beat them because they had no idea what I was doing. Tekken 8 lost so much of its identity, and I tried to voice my concern to the community, but I was met with dismissive comment from people brand new to the series who had jumped on the bandwagon and wanted to act like they knew what Tekken was like before. Criticism that could have helped the game got drowned out, and eventually I dropped Tekken 8, followed by my friend who couldn't stand what the game had become following close behind me. 

As a community, we feel dejected. Tekken is too easy now. They made every character beginner friendly but took out all of the hardest things in Tekken that you could learn. Player expression was gutted, as you probably have heard many people say, but its true. I've never seen someone in Tekken 8 do something that left me in awe and made me want to jump in and practice it, because its not difficult. Anybody who practices the game could do what any pro can currently do, and there's nothing skill-wise that can separate us. And unfortunately, our criticism and pleads didn't just get drowned out, but they got actively ignored by the developers. The devs only wanted to listen to the people who would sing Tekken 8's praise, and in response to everybody begging them to fix the game, they turned around and finished the job, thoroughly destroying the game with this second season. I'll admit, I haven't played the second season, so don't think I'm claiming something I'm not, but it doesn't require you to play it for you to know how bad their decisions were. They nerfed the already gutted movement system and doubled down on aggressive gameplay, to the point where you can't even sidestep mids. Oki is practically nonexistent. Defense is practically nonexistent. Its barely even a fighting game anymore. Its just a rushdown simulator, seeing who can press buttons faster than the other before their healthbars disappear. And the devs hear the outcries of their fanbase and would rather tell them to stop complaining, while thanking the few contrarians who defend the game who get proven to not even play it. 

Let's face it, if the devs don't want to hear from us, then they don't want us here. Fine by me. I treated Tekken like a party game in the beginning, but grew to respect it when I saw how much time and focus I could put into it to improve my gameplay. Now, all people do is treat Tekken like a party game, and they don't ever grow out of that mindset because they're rewarded for doing so. So maybe Tekken is a party game now. This isn't the game I dedicated over a year to improving myself on. That game was left behind, just like we have been now. Tekken is dead.

To preface: I am a complete newcomer to fighting games, all of my thoughts here are from the perspective of someone who has no frame of reference from previous Tekken games. I watched all of the cutscenes summarizing previous games, but even with that the writing was simply abysmal. Extremely generic anime writing with very little depth to any of the characters. Annoyingly, the story mode did not offer much in the way of a tutorial, so most of my learning was pausing at the start of a fight and scrolling through the move lists. The character episodes were even less, you got a brief introductory cutscene, a few fights, than an end cutscene, without adding much more depth to the characters.

Arcade Quest - To be perfectly honest, arcade quest might as well have been the real story mode. It was better in basically every way. A more in-depth tutorial that focuses on whatever character you're playing, a sense of progression as you travel to different arcades fighting stronger and stronger bots (even if they're absolute garbage once you start learning your fundamentals). The writing is still generic as hell of course, but it was fun.

Tekken Ball - Tried it once, didn't care for it... that's all.

Fight Lounge - Seems like an interesting way to introduce a more social aspect to the game. You can chat with people, play against them over and over, and even practice with other players which is really cool. The main downside though is that playing against people is clunky, you have to go to a set of machines, go through a loading screen into a queue, to then "match" against the person. It's very awkward, slow, and unintuitive.

Customization - The customization is alright. I like the ability to freely change parts of an item/clothing to any color you want, and it's a feature I wish more character creators would adopt. The amount of items you can equip is a bit underwhelming, options for facial features like hairstyles and eye colors are especially limited, and the inability to add or tweak things on full body outfits feels rather restrictive. Still, it gives enough creative freedom to pull off some really good looking and/or goofy outfits, as well as cosplays.

Unfortunately, this is not the case for Tekken 8. You have a battlepass, and paid characters and stages. Making people pay for decades-old characters in a $70 game is criminal, and I hate that ♥♥♥♥ like this is normalized in the gaming industry as a whole. Hell, the worst part for me is that you can't even choose the characters in practice mode if you don't own them, so you can't even lab them unless you have somebody willing to practice online with you.

Practice/Replays - The practice mode is phenomenal. The sheer amount of options and settings you can adjust allows you to practice any scenario, positioning, combo, punish, etc. Additionally, the ability to view replays, as well as take control while watching them is a fantastic. A very well thought-out mode.

Quickplay/Ranked - Okay, time for the real meat of the game. Starting out, I got my ass handed to me, as was expected. I slowly worked my way up to Garyu over the course of a few months as I learned a character or two, slowly working on my fundamentals and figuring out how to stop getting hit by stupid ♥♥♥♥. The learning process was extremely fun, getting a feel for the game's movement and applying more moves and combos into real matches was a blast. The ability to infinitely rematch in quickplay was a much needed addition, as it allowed me and a complete stranger to keep beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other while learning our characters' matchup, this was peak enjoyment of the game for me. Unfortunately, reaching the Garyu/Shinryu threshold is where issues with the game became more prevalent.

I understand that much of the game's population is within orange and red ranks, but the skill disparity just doesn't make sense. Sometimes I would get matched up against what felt like green ranks who didn't understand frames and just button mash as you obliterate them. Other times, I would get matched up against what felt like blue ranks who promptly beat my ass. They ducked every high and grab, blocked or parried every low, performed insane wall-carry combos, etc. I'm not sure if smurfing is that prevalent or red ranks are just THAT wide in the range of skill, but matches like these became so common that it just wasn't fun.

Additionally, reaching Garyu is where the game's aggressive nature became much more prevalent. I met more people that would just absolutely rush me down with characters like Nina, Heihachi, and Reina with constant plus on block strings and 50/50s. Now let me say, I understand that these are mostly knowledge checks. I understand that each of these characters have gaps where you can sidestep, jab, crouch, etc to get out of the rush. It feels like red ranks are a wall that halts all of your momentum until you decide to start extensively labbing, it was a very sudden difficulty spike and smothered out a lot of the enjoyment I was having with the game.

Now, the above wouldn't bother me nearly as much if most of these issues didn't seep into Quickplay, but they do. Huge skill disparity, some characters forcing you to adapt or die, relatively common lagswitching and plugging. It all just feels like a coin toss as to whether or not I'm going to actually enjoy a match. A fast, hyperarmor, high damage move that ignores all hits and throws and forces you to watch a cutscene is not fun.
